UK Students Argue For The Legalization of Cannabis

March , 1998

Birmingham SUN

DECRIMINALISE CANNABIS

By Lee Palmer and Paul Douglass

THE decriminalisation and legalisation of cannabis is a subject which has, in recent years, had rather a low profile in the press and in parliament.

Lee Palmer and Paul Douglass investigate the benefits and drawbacks of decriminalising cannabis, a drug that is considered by far the most dangerous in terms of its effects on the authorities.

However, with the launch of its "Decriminalise Cannabis" campaign in late September of last year, the Independent on Sunday has forced this issue once more into the public and political arenas for the first time in 25 years, with widespread support across the media. Publications that have expressed their agreement with this campaign include "The New Statesman", "Melody Maker", "The Daily Express" and "The Daily Mirror." Indeed, the subsequent conference organised by the IoS and held at the Queen Elizabeth II Conference Centre last December proved just how keen some MPs, doctors, police officers, regular cannabis smokers and MS sufferers were to discuss the aspects of its use and the reasons behind its present prohibition.

A conspicuous absentee from the conference was the Home Secretary, Jack Straw, who, having been invited more than a month earlier, claimed to have a full diary. In his letter to the IoS he also added, somewhat ambivalently, that although he was willing to debate this matter, the position of the Government was clear: "We are against the legalisation of cannabis." This standpoint is considered by a large number of young people to be at best hypocritical (that is to say, it has been imposed by middle-aged politicians who indulge their own tastes for tobacco and alcohol, and yet will not allow others to use cannabis as a personal preference) and at worst repressive (denying the individual the right to be happy, whilst doing no harm to others).

In a country where more than 25 million prescriptions for tranquillisers are written each year, it is a sad state of affairs that a naturally-occurring drug which induces relaxation and relieves personal tensions should be outlawed. The medical benefits of cannabis are numerous and have been well documented for thousands of years: the first recorded use can be found in a Chinese pharmacopoeia dating from around 2737 B.C. In 1890, Russell Reynolds wrote in his paper on the therapeutic uses of cannabis that "...when pure and administered carefully it is one of the most valuable medicines we possess." It was praised for its effect in alleviating pain, migraine, insomnia, cramps and even difficult childbirth; it can serve as either a stimulant or a sedative.

In a British Department of Health and Social Security paper, prepared by Sir Aubrey Lewis in 1970, it states that "...pot heads believe themselves to be intelligent, daring, cool-headed, worthy of respect, and they do not resort to violence..." (a large problem connected to alcohol); that "...they remain at school or at work and engage in athletics..."; and that pot also "increases the pleasure of sexual intercourse." So, rumours that it engenders a motivational lethargy in smokers of the drug is purely a matter to do with the individuals concerned.

Similarly, anxieties that decriminalisation would bring about an increased burden upon the Social Security of this country are equally without foundation. Since most of those who claim benefit and smoke dope were receiving their money before taking up consumption of the drug, these political problems cannot be attributed to cannabis.

Prohibition of the drug should, therefore, be reviewed and researched solely on consideration of its relevance to health. Many are convinced that marijuana is an addictive "gateway" drug and that its legalisation would not only increase its number of consumers but also make people want to try harder illegal drugs in an effort to look cool by being outside the law. This case too is without evidence: both alcohol and nicotine are more addictive than cannabis, and nicotine is in fact, weight for weight, more addictive than heroin. In the same respect, alcohol is more of a gateway to heroin than cannabis; the only link between cannabis and heroin being that both are often supplied by the same dealer. Studies in Holland also show that since the relaxation of the laws in that country, there has been no significant increase in its number of hard drug addicts. (Ed. note: Actually, there has been a significant drop! See Comparison of drug addiction levels in various European countries. )

So, what now? The government would argue that there are further problems with regulation and taxation. In this respect, decriminalisation is not viable, as it would still be illegal to cultivate plants and drug dealers would still be able to fix prices. Instead, a situation similar to the one in the Netherlands is the only realistic solution: coffee-shops in Amsterdam are permitted to sell quantities of soft drugs under local laws for consumption on the premises, whilst the owners responsibly discuss the types of weed for sale with prospective buyers prior to the point of purchase.
